MOLD DISCLOSURE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Toxic Mold Protection Act of 2001 (Health & Safety Code §§ 26100-26157) as it may apply to the property at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. It states what California law provides on this subject, including the ways the Act's own disclosure duties are conditioned on regulatory action that this document reports has not, as of the date below, been shown to have occurred. It does not authorize, direct, or prohibit any particular disclosure, and it does not tell either Pat Morgan or Jordan Lee what to do about any specific condition at the property.

THE TOXIC MOLD PROTECTION ACT AND THE DEPARTMENT'S ROLE
California's Health and Safety Code chapter on toxic mold is officially titled the Toxic Mold Protection Act of 2001. The Act designates the department -- defined in the statute as the State Department of Health Services -- as the lead agency for adopting permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments, mold identification and remediation efforts, and guidelines for what constitutes mold infestation. In a later, separate statutory reorganization, the State Department of Public Health was made the successor to, and vested with, the duties and functions of the former State Department of Health Services as they relate to public health. Before the department is required to adopt permissible exposure limits, the statute first directs it to consider whether doing so is feasible.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the Toxic Mold Protection Act of 2001."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26100 (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, short title of the Act (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26100.)
  "“Department” means the State Department of Health Services, designated as the lead agency in the adoption of permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments, mold identification and remediation efforts, and the development of guidelines for the determination of what constitutes mold infestation."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26101(e) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, definition of "department" as lead agency (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26101.)
  "the State Department of Public Health shall succeed to and be vested with all the duties, powers, purposes, functions, responsibilities, and jurisdiction of the former State Department of Health Services as they relate to public health"
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 131050(a) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, State Department of Public Health as successor to the State Department of Health Services for public health functions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=131050.)
  "The department shall consider the feasibility of adopting permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26102 (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, feasibility study required before adopting exposure limits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26102.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides on toxic mold regulation -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's property. The two citations to Health & Safety Code § 26101 and § 26102 are subsections/sections within the same chapter of the same code and are not independent sources of each other; the citation to § 131050 is a separate, independently enacted statutory section addressing the 2007 state health-agency reorganization, offered as a genuinely independent source for the successor-agency point (not as corroboration of §§ 26101-26102). This document does not independently verify the department's current internal organization, name, or any regulations it may have adopted outside the statutory text itself -- only the statutory text was checked.

THE ACT'S STANDARDS, GUIDELINES, AND FUNDING-CONTINGENT STRUCTURE
The Act's substantive framework -- permissible exposure limits, health-threat assessment standards, and identification and remediation guidelines -- is not self-executing. By the statute's own terms, the department is only required to adopt permissible exposure limits "if the department finds that adopting permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments is feasible." Several of the Act's own disclosure provisions, including the residential landlord disclosure duty, then state that their own requirements "shall not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 that occurs at least six months after the department adopts standards pursuant to Sections 26103 and 26105 and develops guidelines pursuant to Section 26130" -- meaning those specific disclosure duties are, by the statute's own text, contingent on the department having first adopted those standards and guidelines. Separately, the Act's implementation article states that the entire chapter "shall be implemented only to the extent that the department determines that funds are available for the implementation of this chapter."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) If the department finds that adopting permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments is feasible, the department, in consultation with the task force convened pursuant to Section 26101.7, shall:"
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26103(a) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, exposure limits conditioned on a feasibility finding (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26103.)
  "The department, in consultation with the task force convened pursuant to Section 26101.7, shall adopt practical standards to assess the health threat posed by the presence of mold, both visible and invisible or hidden, in an indoor environment."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26105(a) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, department's duty to adopt health-threat assessment standards (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26105.)
  "The requirements of this section shall not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 that occurs at least six months after the department adopts standards pursuant to Sections 26103 and 26105 and develops guidelines pursuant to Section 26130."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26147(e) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, residential landlord disclosure duty delayed until standards and guidelines are adopted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26147.)
  "This chapter shall be implemented only to the extent that the department determines that funds are available for the implementation of this chapter."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26156 (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, funding-contingent implementation of the entire chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26156.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's property. The four citations below are to four different, independently enacted statutory sections within the same chapter (§§ 26102, 26103, 26147, 26156), not different subdivisions of one section, and are treated here as separate sources; note, however, that the quoted "shall not apply until..." triggering sentence in § 26147(e) recurs, in essentially identical wording, in several other sections of the same Article 4 (including §§ 26140(d), 26141(e), 26142(b), 26143(b), 26145(b), and 26146(d)) -- this document cites only the § 26147 instance as representative rather than treating each repetition as an independently corroborating source. This document reports what the statutory text itself says about the conditions under which the department's standards, guidelines, and the resulting disclosure duties take effect; it does not independently verify -- from the department's own current regulations, website, or any other source outside this statutory text -- whether the department has in fact adopted permissible exposure limits, assessment standards, or guidelines as of the checked date. A reader who needs to know the department's current regulatory status should consult the department directly or its current regulations, not this document.

RESIDENTIAL LANDLORD DISCLOSURE OF KNOWN MOLD
Subject to the conditions described elsewhere in this information sheet, California law requires a residential landlord to provide written disclosure to prospective and current tenants of an affected unit when the landlord "knows, or has reasonable cause to believe," that mold -- visible or hidden -- is present that affects the unit or building and either exceeds the permissible exposure limits established under Section 26103 or poses a health threat under the department's guidelines developed under Section 26105. A residential landlord is not required to conduct air or surface testing to determine whether mold exceeds those exposure limits. Where the duty applies, written disclosure must be provided to prospective tenants before they enter into the rental or lease agreement, and to current tenants of an affected unit as soon as reasonably practical. A residential landlord is exempt from the disclosure duty to prospective tenants if the mold was remediated according to the department's mold remediation guidelines developed under Section 26130.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Subject to subdivisions (b), (d), and (e), residential landlords shall provide written disclosure to prospective and current tenants of the affected units as specified in subdivision (b) when the residential landlord knows, or has reasonable cause to believe, that mold, both visible and invisible or hidden, is present that affects the unit or the building and the mold either exceeds the permissible exposure limits to molds established by subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) of Section 26103 or poses a health threat according to the department’s guidelines as developed pursuant to Section 26105."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26147(a) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, the core residential landlord disclosure duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26147.)
  "(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a residential landlord shall not be required to conduct air or surface tests of units or buildings to determine whether the presence of molds exceeds the permissible exposure limits to molds established by subdivisions (a) and (b) of Section 26103."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26147(b) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, no air or surface testing required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26147.)
  "(c) The written disclosure required by subdivision (a) shall be provided: (1) To prospective tenants prior to entering into the rental or lease agreement. (2) To current tenants in affected units as soon as is reasonably practical."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26147(c) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, timing of the written disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26147.)
  "(d) A residential landlord shall be exempt from providing written disclosure to prospective tenants pursuant to this section if the presence of mold was remediated according to the mold remediation guidelines developed by the department pursuant to Section 26130."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26147(d) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, exemption where mold was already remediated (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26147.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a residential landlord's mold disclosure duty -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy. All four citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 26147) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was sought for the elements of this specific duty. As described in this document's other clauses, § 26147(e) itself states that these requirements do not apply until at least six months after the department has adopted standards under Sections 26103 and 26105 and developed guidelines under Section 26130 -- a condition this document does not independently verify has been satisfied. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine whether any specific landlord knew or had reasonable cause to believe mold was present, or whether any specific disclosure was required or adequate.

RESIDENTIAL LANDLORD CONSUMER BOOKLET DISCLOSURE
Separately from the disclosure duty described elsewhere in this information sheet, California law also directs residential landlords to provide prospective tenants with written disclosure of the potential health risks and health impact that may result from mold exposure, by distributing a consumer-oriented booklet developed and disseminated by the department, before the tenant enters into the rental or lease agreement. This booklet-distribution duty, like the disclosure duty described elsewhere in this information sheet, does not apply until at least six months after the department approves the consumer-oriented booklet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Residential landlords shall provide written disclosure to prospective tenants of the potential health risks and the health impact that may result from exposure to mold by distributing a consumer-oriented booklet developed and disseminated by the department."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26148(a) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, residential landlord consumer-booklet disclosure duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26148.)
  "(c) The requirements of this section shall not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 that occurs at least six months after the department approves the consumer-oriented booklet, as described in subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26148(c) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, booklet duty delayed until department approves the booklet (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26148.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a residential landlord's booklet-disclosure duty -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy. The two citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 26148) rather than independently authored sources. This document does not independently verify whether the department has in fact approved a consumer-oriented booklet as of the checked date -- only the statutory text conditioning the duty on that approval was checked. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine whether any specific landlord's booklet-distribution duty has taken effect.

SCOPE: THE ACT'S SALE-RELATED DISCLOSURE DUTY COVERS COMMERCIAL AND INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY, NOT RESIDENTIAL SALES
The Act's specific disclosure duty tied to a property sale applies to a "seller or transferor of commercial or industrial real property," who must disclose known mold meeting the same exceeds-limits-or-health-threat standard described elsewhere in this information sheet to prospective buyers as soon as practicable before transfer of title. The Act does not contain a parallel, mold-specific disclosure section addressed to the seller of residential real property. The Act separately states that nothing in its disclosure article relieves any seller, transferor, lessor, agent, landlord, or tenant of other existing legal obligations, including specified Civil Code duties and any other duties under common law, and that nothing in the article affects the existing obligation of parties to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose facts materially affecting the value and desirability of the property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Subject to subdivisions (b), (c), and (d), a seller or transferor of commercial or industrial real property shall provide written disclosure to prospective buyers as soon as practicable before the transfer of title when the seller or transferor knows of the presence of mold, both visible and invisible or hidden, that affects the unit or building and the mold either exceeds permissible exposure limits to molds established by subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) of Section 26103 or poses a health threat, according to the department’s guidelines as developed pursuant to Section 26105."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26140(a) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, commercial or industrial seller/transferor disclosure duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26140.)
  "(a) Nothing in this article shall relieve a seller, transferor, lessor, agent, landlord, or tenant from any responsibility for compliance with other obligations, laws, ordinances, codes, or regulations, including but not limited to the duties outlined in Sections 1941 and 1941.1 of the Civil Code and any other duties provided for under common law."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26149(a) (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, other legal obligations preserved (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26149.)
  "Nothing in this article shall affect the existing obligations of the parties or transferor to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose any facts materially affecting the value and desirability of the property, including, but not limited to, the physical conditions of the property and previously received reports of physical inspections noted on the disclosure form set forth in Section 1102.6 or 1102.6a of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26150 (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, existing real estate contract disclosure obligations preserved (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26150.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's transaction. The three citations below are to three different, independently enacted statutory sections within the same Article 4 (§§ 26140, 26149, 26150), not subdivisions of one section, and are treated here as separate sources. This document reports only that the Act's own mold-specific sale-disclosure section names commercial and industrial property, and that the Act separately preserves other, non-Act disclosure obligations without describing what those other obligations are; it does not independently verify the content, scope, or applicability of any other disclosure statute (including the Civil Code sections referenced in §§ 26149-26150) to a residential sale, and does not address whether or how a residential seller's general disclosure duties might reach a known mold condition. This document is informational only and does not determine any party's disclosure obligations in a specific transaction.

LIABILITY LIMITATION AND ENFORCEMENT
California law limits liability for an error, inaccuracy, or omission in information delivered under the Act's disclosure article: neither the transferor nor any listing or selling agent is liable for such an error if it was not within their personal knowledge, or was based on information timely provided by public agencies or by other persons delivering a report or opinion within the scope of their professional license or expertise, provided ordinary care was exercised in obtaining and transmitting the information. On enforcement, designated public health officers, code enforcement officers, environmental health officers, city attorneys, and other appropriate government entities may respond to complaints about mold and enforce the disclosure requirements described elsewhere in this information sheet. No penalty may be assessed against an owner for failure to disclose under the residential landlord disclosure section if the owner provides disclosure to tenants in a form that substantially conforms to the disclosure form the department develops.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Neither the transferor nor any listing or selling agent shall be held liable for any error, inaccuracy, or omission of any information delivered pursuant to this article if the error, inaccuracy, or omission was not within the personal knowledge of the transferor, or the listing or selling agent, or was based on information timely provided by public agencies, or by other persons providing relevant information by delivery of a report or opinion prepared by an expert dealing with matters within the relevant scope of the professional’s license or expertise, and ordinary care was exercised in obtaining and transmitting it."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26153 (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, liability limitation for good-faith errors or omissions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26153.)
  "No penalty shall be assessed against an owner for failure to disclose under Section 26147 where the owner provides disclosure to the tenants in a form that substantially conforms to the disclosure form developed by the department."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26154 (California Legislative Information text), Health and Safety Code, no penalty for substantially conforming disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=26154.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides on liability limitation and enforcement for mold disclosures -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's property. The two citations below are to two different, independently enacted statutory sections (§§ 26153 and 26154), not subdivisions of one section, and are treated here as separate sources. This document does not independently verify whether the department has adopted the disclosure form or the "disclosure enforcement guidelines" that § 26154 itself makes a precondition to local enforcement authority, nor does it address any liability theory outside this specific statutory liability limitation (such as common-law negligence, fraud, or habitability claims, or liability under the Civil Code duties preserved by §§ 26149-26150). This document is informational only; it does not itself determine whether any specific error, omission, or disclosure was made with ordinary care, or whether any specific disclosure substantially conforms to a department-developed form.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding mold disclosure under California's Toxic Mold Protection Act of 2001, concerning the property at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee, states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any specific mold condition or disclosure question.

The Act separately states that nothing in its disclosure article relieves any seller, transferor, lessor, agent, landlord, or tenant of other existing legal obligations, including specified Civil Code duties and any other duties under common law, and that nothing in the article affects the existing obligation of parties to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose facts materially affecting the value and desirability of the property.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26140(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, commercial or industrial seller/transferor disclosure duty
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivisions (b), (c), and (d), a seller or transferor of commercial or industrial real property shall provide written disclosure to prospective buyers as soon as practicable before the transfer of title when the seller or transferor knows of the presence of mold, both visible and invisible or hidden, that affects the unit or building and the mold either exceeds permissible exposure limits to molds established by subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) of Section 26103 or poses a health threat, according to the department’s guidelines as developed pursuant to Section 26105.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26149(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, other legal obligations preserved
citations.quote: (a) Nothing in this article shall relieve a seller, transferor, lessor, agent, landlord, or tenant from any responsibility for compliance with other obligations, laws, ordinances, codes, or regulations, including but not limited to the duties outlined in Sections 1941 and 1941.1 of the Civil Code and any other duties provided for under common law.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26150 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, existing real estate contract disclosure obligations preserved
citations.quote: Nothing in this article shall affect the existing obligations of the parties or transferor to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose any facts materially affecting the value and desirability of the property, including, but not limited to, the physical conditions of the property and previously received reports of physical inspections noted on the disclosure form set forth in Section 1102.6 or 1102.6a of the Civil Code.

The three citations below are to three different, independently enacted statutory sections within the same Article 4 (§§ 26140, 26149, 26150), not subdivisions of one section, and are treated here as separate sources. This document reports only that the Act's own mold-specific sale-disclosure section names commercial and industrial property, and that the Act separately preserves other, non-Act disclosure obligations without describing what those other obligations are; it does not independently verify the content, scope, or applicability of any other disclosure statute (including the Civil Code sections referenced in §§ 26149-26150) to a residential sale, and does not address whether or how a residential seller's general disclosure duties might reach a known mold condition. This document is informational only and does not determine any party's disclosure obligations in a specific transaction.

expectedJSON.body: California law limits liability for an error, inaccuracy, or omission in information delivered under the Act's disclosure article: neither the transferor nor any listing or selling agent is liable for such an error if it was not within their personal knowledge, or was based on information timely provided by public agencies or by other persons delivering a report or opinion within the scope of their professional license or expertise, provided ordinary care was exercised in obtaining and transmitting the information. On enforcement, designated public health officers, code enforcement officers, environmental health officers, city attorneys, and other appropriate government entities may respond to complaints about mold and enforce the disclosure requirements described elsewhere in this information sheet. No penalty may be assessed against an owner for failure to disclose under the residential landlord disclosure section if the owner provides disclosure to tenants in a form that substantially conforms to the disclosure form the department develops.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26153 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, liability limitation for good-faith errors or omissions
citations.quote: Neither the transferor nor any listing or selling agent shall be held liable for any error, inaccuracy, or omission of any information delivered pursuant to this article if the error, inaccuracy, or omission was not within the personal knowledge of the transferor, or the listing or selling agent, or was based on information timely provided by public agencies, or by other persons providing relevant information by delivery of a report or opinion prepared by an expert dealing with matters within the relevant scope of the professional’s license or expertise, and ordinary care was exercised in obtaining and transmitting it.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26154 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, no penalty for substantially conforming disclosure
citations.quote: No penalty shall be assessed against an owner for failure to disclose under Section 26147 where the owner provides disclosure to the tenants in a form that substantially conforms to the disclosure form developed by the department.
